hints: Look closely at the word cristae. These are the folded inner membranes inside a mitochondrion, packed very, very close together. What do you need to be able to do to see them as separate lines?
Think resolution versus magnification. A light microscope cannot separate two points closer than about 200 nm. Which statement links this limit to why a student daylight microscope fails?
walkthrough:
**Spot what we need to see**

Think like a biologist for a moment. Cristae are tiny folds of membrane, only a few nanometres thick and very close together.

To see them, we do not just need a bigger image, we need to see two very close membranes as two separate lines.

**Recall the resolution limit**

Resolution is the ability to distinguish two points that are very close together as separate.

For a light microscope using daylight, the limit is about:
$$ \text{resolution limit} \approx 200 \, nm $$ 
Anything closer together than this will blur into one fuzzy structure, no matter how much you magnify it.

**Apply to the options**

The cristae membranes are separated by less than this 200 nm limit, so a student light microscope simply cannot resolve them.

An electron microscope uses a beam with a much shorter wavelength, giving much higher resolution. So the correct explanation is that the resolution of the student daylight microscope is too low.

options.A: It is true electron microscopes magnify more, but magnification alone just makes a blurry image bigger. It does not explain why we must use it, resolution does.
options.B: This is back to front. If the membranes were more than 200 nm apart, a light microscope could resolve them and we would not need an electron microscope.
options.C: Well done, this is the key idea. The student daylight microscope has too low a resolution (limited to about 200 nm) to separate the closely packed cristae membranes.
options.D: This gets the physics wrong. The wavelength of an electron beam is much shorter than light, and it is this short wavelength that gives high resolution.
